prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow frequency standards at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B044 to B052, Katori and Ye. The chair asked what my objection to the clock is beyond overlap and timing, and after the first round I have to say that there is none. My seventh place at the opening rested on exactly those two points, and neither survives the exchange. On overlap, Kroll and Lindroth give the physical distinction I had not weighted properly: the comb of 2005 solved the counting of optical cycles, and the ion control of 2012 concerned a single trapped particle, whereas the lattice clock uses a magic-wavelength condition that cancels the light shift while Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects, so that a large ensemble is interrogated in parallel. That is a different mechanism with a different payoff, and it shows in the stability and accuracy reached, about 1e-18, reproduced by independent laboratories and on more than one species. On timing, I agree that a prize should not be hostage to an administrative decision on the second; the physics is confirmed now. The attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori supplied the concept and early realisation, and Ye took it to the accuracy and many-body frontier. By contrast my own candidate B044 still has four names for three places, and Zoller versus Esslinger cannot be settled from the supplied evidence. I still think quantum simulation is the more conceptually original line, but a prize that must name at most three people should be judged on what can be credited cleanly, and the clock clears that bar while B044 does not.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that the clock is still an increment inside a precision-spectroscopy lineage honoured in 2005 and 2012, and it is not a new class of phenomena in the sense that B044 or B021 are. I accept that this is a difference of degree and a matter of how the citation is worded; it has to name the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its realisation and not optical clocks in general. The two-name credit also leaves out PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Tokyo contributors such as Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemke and Hinkley, and several members recall the priority details from memory, as do I. Finally, the redefinition of the second is unfinished, so the societal payoff is prospective, although I do not regard that as a reason to wait. If the committee wants a prize whose main merit is breadth of new physics and not precision, B044 remains the better answer in principle.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock solves a different physical problem from the comb, namely interrogating many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength without Doppler, recoil or light-shift penalties, and that the prize should not wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me. I had grouped the clock with the comb as one metrology lineage, and your distinction between counting cycles and controlling the systematic shifts of a large ensemble is a physical one, not a matter of wording. I accept it, and I also accept your point on timing. Where I would hold you to a standard is the citation: it should carry the magic-wavelength lattice and Lamb-Dicke confinement explicitly, so that the committee is on record as crediting a mechanism and not a general improvement in precision, and I have written mine that way. I still think you and I weigh breadth against measurement-limited advance differently, but that difference no longer decides my vote.

responses.point: Pearce asked why I ranked the clocks seventh, which is a large gap from the other six members, and asked whether this hides a physics concern; he also argued that B044 cannot be attributed within three names.
responses.response: There was no hidden physics concern; the seventh place rested on overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and on the unfinished redefinition of the second, and I now think both were overweighted. I also concede your attribution point on B044. Jaksch and Zoller, Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger cannot be fitted into three names without leaving out someone whom a reader of the history would expect, and I could not settle Zoller versus Esslinger in round 1 either. Your remark that the decisive results on open many-body problems are still arriving also bears on my own uncertainty about whether analogue simulation has produced a decisive result yet. That is the main reason I now place it as an alternative and not as the prize.

responses.point: Danielsson says the allocation problem in B044 is severe, that B052 has no such problem, and that the prize should not be hostage to a metrological decision, while accepting that B044 could be a later prize.
responses.response: I agree on both counts and I take your last sentence as the right way to hold the two together: the difficulty with B044 is partly one of credit, not of merit, so choosing B052 now does not close the door on lattice quantum simulation later. I differ with you only on how clean the clock's overlap with the cold-atom community is, since the same laser-cooling and trapping toolkit sits under both. That is a reason for the citation to be narrow, not a reason against the prize.

responses.point: Eriksson accepts that B052 would be the best fallback if the attribution of B021 is judged irreparable and says the committee should weigh the cleaner credit of the clocks against the broader conceptual novelty of the topological insulators.
responses.response: I would put it the same way, and for me the attribution question has now been decided in favour of B052. My view of B021 is unchanged: the Z2 formulation and the HgTe observation are both mature, but the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that triggered the experiment cannot be credited within three names, and I do not think the 2016 overlap is the deciding point. We therefore disagree about how much that omission costs, but we reach the same fallback. If your concern is conceptual novelty, I share it, which is why I keep B044 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B011 as the most original and least replaceable contribution, but calls B052 the strongest consensus candidate and says she does not think breadth of support should replace merit.
responses.response: I agree that support counts are not a substitute for judgement, and I did not move because six members ranked the clock highly. I moved because the physical objection I held was answered. On B011, I respect that the correctors overcame a real limit in charged-particle optics, but the credit divides between the TEM and STEM lineages and a three-name list cannot cover both, which is the same kind of attribution problem that I am using against B044. I read that as a reason the clock, with its two-name credit, is the more defensible choice.

uncertainties: Whether the magic-wavelength lattice will be seen as a mechanism distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; this depends on the citation wording.
Priority between Katori's proposal and the early strontium demonstrations, and the weight of the PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Tokyo groups; I recall these from memory and have not verified them.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second; I now think not, but I cannot rule out that others will find the timing argument decisive.
Whether lattice quantum simulation (B044) deserves a later prize and with which third name, Zoller or Esslinger.
Whether analogue quantum simulation has yet produced a decisive scientific result or is still a maturing platform.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My documented co-authors and institutions (Gothenburg, Max Planck, Oxford, Freiburg) do not include Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist. My research on statistical physics of complex systems and neural networks is not directly tied to the candidates. My earlier preference for B044 reflects my general interest in many-body and statistical questions and I disclose that I have changed it.
